recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls on transiting consignments at all exit BIPs comply with the requirements of Article 3 of Decision 2000/208/EC in order to verify that the consignments have not been manipulated.

citations.text: In April 2014, the central competent authority in cooperation with Customs approved an instruction for exit checks made by Customs officials outside the working hours of BIPs. Following the newly approved instruction, the BIP staff perform the exit checks of transit consignments during the working hours of the BIPs. Customs are responsible for 9 the exit checks of transit consignments outside the working hours of the BIPs. The instruction is prepared following the requirements of Directive 97/78/EC and Decision 2000/208/EC.

In those cases where the transit checks are done by the BIP staff the seal check is done at the BIP facilities. Outside of working hours, the seal check is done by Customs officials at the Customs control post. In both cases these controls are done following the requirements of Decision 2001/812/EC. The port BIPs visited keep track of exiting transit consignments until they are unloaded into ships for dispatch outside the EU.

The audit team noted that none of the BIPs visited follow the above-mentioned work instruction: a. In the Ploce port, Customs authorities always send the exit transit consignments to the BIP for checks even if the BIP is not working. The consignment then waits until the BIP is open. b. In the Rijeka port, the exit transit checks are always performed by Customs even when the BIP is open. The local agreement to divert from the national instruction (finding 44) is not documented. Central Customs officials confirmed that Customs are obliged to check veterinary seals only in cases defined in the national instruction. This means there is no legal obligation for Customs to check the veterinary seals following the requirements of Article 3 of Decision 2000/208/EC when the BIP is open.

The official controls of exit transit consignments are correctly implemented in the vast majority of cases ensuring that consignments leave the EU territory as required by EU legislation, except for the Rijeka BIP. The different, undocumented implementation of instructions on exit transit controls at this BIP level cannot ensure that the exiting consignments are checked to confirm that they have not been manipulated during transit. 10

recommendations.text: To ensure implementation of the identity check at the warehouses as required by Article 4 of Directive 97/78/EC.

citations.text: A consignment split in the warehouse visited had been rejected by the third country of destination due to a mismatch between the lot number on the boxes and the lot number on the health certificate accompanying the consignment from origin. The competent authority interpreted that there is no legal requirement to check/record the lot numbers of the consignments during the full identity check. This is contrary to the requirements of Article 4(4)(a)(ii) of Directive 97/78/EC. The operator of the warehouse stated it had taken corrective actions and strengthened controls during loading, cross-checking the lot number to match with the information on the health certificate.

The audit team conducted traceability exercises both to trace back and trace forward a randomly selected product in the warehouse. The data from TRACES matched precisely the info provided by the competent authorities' and the operator's records. However, the lot number of the consignment examined did not match that indicated in the original health certificate which accompanied the consignment. This had not been detected during the checks upon arrival at the warehouse, which is not in line with the requirements of Article 4(4)(a)(iii) of Directive 97/78/EC and Article 4 of Decision 2000/571/EC.

There are controls at the warehouses, but identity checks upon arrival at the warehouses do not ensure that mismatches with the certificates are identified. The mismatch with the original certificate means that those goods are (i) accepted for transit without adequate guarantees and (ii) are re-certified incorrectly by EU officials at the time of dispatch. The risk to animal health is mitigated since currently only canned fishery products are stored in the warehouses. Furthermore, the traceability system put in place by the operator allows for the reconciliation of the goods. 5.2.5 Controls at the exit BIP

However, there are some difficulties for staff to implement adequately the official sampling, particularly the sampling frequency and/or protocol in breeders and in laying hen population.

The audit team was informed by the VFSD that in the 2015 annual plan for official controls they forgot to include Salmonella official sampling for all the various poultry populations. However they detected the problem in the course of the year and to remedy the situation a complementary document was prepared. The document indicated the poultry holdings where Salmonella sampling had to be performed in the second half of 2015 and was sent by the VFSD to the regional offices and from there to the branch offices in order to be implemented. The CA informed the audit team that this document could partially cover the official sampling required by the SNCPs in 2015. However, due to limited time available for the branch offices to organise the sampling, an insufficient number of official samples were taken, in particular in breeding and laying hen populations where a higher number of official samples had to be collected.

In the branch offices visited the audit team had the opportunity to confirm that, for the reasons explained above, the official sampling was not carried out with the required frequency in particular in breeders and in laying hen population (see also paragraphs Nos 90 and 103).

During the on-the-spot visits the audit team noted there were some problems concerning the implementation of the official sampling, particularly in the breeding hen population as regards the sampling frequency and in the laying hen population as regards the sampling frequency and the protocol. The audit team also noted that the difference between own-check and official sampling was not very clear to the staff responsible for implementing the SNCPs.

In this regard the VFSD informed the audit team that prior to 2015 all samples taken in the framework of the SNCPs were considered as official samples. However, since 2015 a distinction has been made by the CA between own-check and official sampling in national rules and the SNCPs because the relevant EU legislation stipulates that poultry populations should be sampled at the initiative of the FBO and as part of official controls. The CA explained to the audit team that due to the fact that these changes have taken place recently, the staff is still encountering difficulties in differentiating between the sampling for own-checks and the sampling for official controls and it therefore may happen that some staff does not apply the right sampling scheme.

The audit team noted that although the CA is aware of the issue concerning official sampling i.e. through the supervision of VIs carried out by the CA from central level and heads of regional offices and the monthly reports of Salmonella analysis results sent by the NRL to the CA at central level (see paragraph No 79), and that some corrective actions have been put in place to remedy the situation detected, problems were still present at the time of the current audit.

Moreover, the implementation of the SNCPs is currently compromised because of the lack of information, available to the CAs responsible for implementing the programmes, concerning the number of flocks per holding.

The audit team noted in all the farms visited that official sampling had not been carried out in 2015 and that one official sample taken in 2016 was analysed in a designated laboratory instead of being tested in the NRL as required by the SNCP.

The audit team was provided by the CA with the data of official sampling performed in 2015. According to this data the frequency for official sampling was not in line with EU requirements (six official samples were tested while there were 64 holdings with more than 1,000 birds). The audit team noted in one of the laying hen farms visited that no 17 official samples had been taken in 2015. The CA explained that this fact was due to the mistake made in the 2015 annual planning (see paragraph No 65).

In the majority of cases reviewed by the audit team, the protocol used in official sampling was not in line with point 2.2.2 of Annex to Regulation (EU) No 517/2011 (e.g. in a caged laying hen farm two faecal samples were taken instead of the required three faecal samples and in a free range farm two faeces samples were taken instead of three pairs of boot swaps). National legislation and guidelines necessary to implement EU requirements relevant for the sector audited have been issued and, from a preliminary analysis, they are in line with EU legislation with the exception of the national measures applied to FBOs who 4 process their own milk at farm level. Furthermore, changing facilities/space for storage of cleaning and disinfection agents must be located outside processing areas. At the time of this audit 104 such FBOs, manufacturing dairy products, out of a total number of 472 approved food operators, had been approved and listed by the CCA. citations.text: DAFI stated, that the information in the farm registry is not sufficient to differentiate farms in regards of the microbiological risks of their crop.

Agricultural inspectors are informed by letter about the planned controls to be conducted in a given year. In 2017 and 2018 the number of FNAO controls was set at ten per Agricultural Inspector in charge of food safety. Inspectors stated that they would need to do an effortful individual research to identify farms with the riskiest crops. Therefore, the inspectors met by the audit team choose to add the controls on microbiological risk to the controls of FBOs which were selected for plant protection controls.
The only selection criterion provided by DAFI to the inspectors was the size of farm to be taken into account.

However, regarding primary production, the official control system is not risk based regarding microbiological contamination. Moreover, the selection of farms is based on criteria for controls on plant protection and not specific for microbiological risks. This is not in line with Article 3(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.4 Implementation of Official Controls over FBO's Obligations Legal requirements Article 10(2)(b)(i), 10(2)(c) and 10(2)(d), and Article 15(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, Articles 4, Article 5, Article 6, Article 7, Article 8, Annex I and Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Article 3 of Regulation (EU) No 208/2013, Regulation (EU) No 211/2013, Article 1 and Annex I of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. citations.text: There are 17 staff on central level and around 70 inspectors in charge of official controls for primary production. Around 30 are dedicated to food safety controls. They have at least a bachelor degree with additional training for food safety issues. Inspectors had received training on microbiological risks at primary production stage in 2017. However, some staff showed a lack of knowledge regarding basic food hygiene requirements in FNAO and legal obligations for sprouting businesses (see chapter 5.2.4).

The staff performing official controls for primary production are trained regarding the reduction of microbiological risks at primary production and in sprout production. However, the training of some inspectors did not enable them to undertake their duties with full competence which is not in line with Articles 4 (2)(a) and 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. 5.2.2 Registration / Approval of Food Establishments Legal requirements Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 852/204, Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 210/2013 and Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 5 Findings Registration of primary producers

The audit team verified the approval files of both sprout-producing establishments and noticed that for one sprouting establishment a sampling plan was required and delivered after the inspection. The analytical results provided, however, did not cover the bacteria required by the sampling plane, in particular no analyses for STEC. The approval, however has been granted. In addition, during the on-site visit several non-compliances have been observed (see chapter 5.2.4). Conclusions on Registration / Approval of Food Establishments

There is a system in place for approval of sprouting establishments aimed at ensuring that applicant FBOs meet the relevant requirements, but this system does not ensure that non-compliances have been rectified before the approval is granted. 5.2.3 Organisation and Scope of Official Controls Legal requirements Article 17 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and Articles 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 Findings Primary producers and sprouting business

The checklist covers all necessary items, however the audit team noted, that during the inspection several non-compliances were not noted by the inspectors: Field and farm toilets without soap, disinfection, towels; Dysfunctional toilets, carton boards on toilet floors; Missing staff instructions and warning signs for hand washing and disinfection in staff toilets; Wooden boxes stored in open air for the harvest of leafy vegetables; Potential risky use of standing water and sponges to treat the cutting surface of lettuce; Presence of bird nests and excrements in packaging and food storage area; Dirty packing / sorting machines said to be unused, but not labelled or identified as such, dirty packaging material (cartoon boxes). Sprout-producing establishments

There are two sprout producers serving the national market. They are approved by DAFI and inspected once a year using a checklist with no non-compliances. Both were visited by the audit team, witnessing the CA inspections. The inspector carrying out the inspection did not note, however, that the facilities showed notable hygiene shortcomings (e.g. non-washable surfaces, dirty hand-shower, not easy to clean and disinfect surfaces in the production area).

Regarding seeds for sprouting, both FBO and CA were not aware of the certification requirements for seeds imported from third countries. The seeds were purchased in other Member States and considered as EU produce. The analytical testing of seeds as 10 required by Regulation (EC) 2073/2005 was not done. The audit team was informed by the CCA that a derogation for pre-testing was in place, but there was no written evidence available. DAFI stated that the derogations were given formless and without further conditions because of the small size of the seed consignments received by the FBOs.

Regarding the final produce, the FBOs did analyse their final produce systematically, but one of them did not check for Listeria, and the other one not for STEC as required. Freezing/Packing Establishments

There is an official control system in place along the FNAO production chain. The implementation at primary production, however, shows a number of gaps, notably related to provision of training and specific instructions (i.e. what are relevant non- compliances regarding the hygiene of staff, safe handling of food and suitable facilities). Therefore, significant non-compliances were not detected. Thus, non- compliant products might be undetected and the correct application of the relevant legislation might not be enforced.

Regarding the sprouting businesses the inspectors did not verify effectively compliance of import certificates because they were not familiar with the certification and traceability requirements established in Regulations (EU) Nos 208/2013 and 211/2013. Furthermore, inspectors did not verify that the own checks contained the analyses of sprouts for Listeria monocytogenes and STEC. Thus, the implementation of official controls on sprout producers is not sufficiently effective in verifying and, as appropriate, enforcing applicable hygiene rules.

The CA did grant informally derogations for the pre-testing of seeds of sprouting without any conditions which is not in line with the rules and criteria laid down in Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 for seeds for sprouting. Thus, non-compliant products might be placed on the market and could pose a health risk for the consumers. 5.2.5 Official Sampling Procedures Legal requirements Article 11 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Annex I, Chapter 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 Findings

citations.text: Training of official staff has not been sufficient for keeping them up-to-date in their area, which does not meet the requirement laid down in Article 6(a) and (b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. In addition, there are no documented procedures (containing information and instructions for staff performing official controls in the area of rabies eradication), that meet the requirements laid down in Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Training on the implementation of the rabies eradication programme was last organised by the CCA in 2012, before the start of the nationwide ORV programme. Since then, no additional training has been organised and the only available instructions are the national legal acts. There were no instructions or guidelines for staff of the AVOs on how to determine which of the wild animals delivered dead to the veterinary station should be submitted for rabies testing under the passive surveillance programme (see also finding 50). 5 The official staff interviewed did not all apply the same definitions for animals submitted for testing under the passive surveillance and were not aware that foxes and jackals found dead should be seen as indicator animals and tested for rabies. There were no instructions or guidelines for official staff in charge of controls on the storage conditions for oral vaccine baits, the aerial distribution of vaccine, or the implementation of the monitoring and surveillance programmes by AVOs. Conclusions on competent authorities

National legislation provides a sound legal basis for all relevant aspects of the rabies eradication programme, and the division of tasks among the Departments in the VFSD provides a good basis for effective implementation of the rabies eradication. However, due to the lack of up-to-date training, information and instructions for official staff and authorised veterinary organisations, and the omission of important tasks in the annual inspection plan for veterinary inspectors, important components of the rabies eradication programme have not been adequately implemented and controlled.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should provide port veterinarians with sufficient information and instructions, as required by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, to carry out official controls at the exit point at the port.

citations.text: The procedures did not indicate that there needs to be a transporter for the sea journey who is established, or in the case that the applicant is established in a non-EU country, represented in the Member State (Article 10(1) of the Regulation). As a result port inspectors did not detect the absence of an authorised transporter responsible for the journey by sea (which should be in box 6.4 of section 1 of the journey logs). In practice, the port veterinarians make all requests regarding fulfilling the legal requirements for the export of animals to a forwarding agent, or the captain of the livestock vessel, although the competent authority has not defined if either of these actors have any legal responsibilities in relation to the welfare of animals during transport.

The written procedures did not include instructions to take into account the judgement of the European Court of Justice in case C-424/13: Zuchtvieh3 (hereafter "the Zuchtvieh ruling") when checking journey logs; i.e. the organiser of the journey has to submit a journey log which is realistic and compliant with the Regulation up to the destination, including the stages of the journey which take place outside the EU.

The officials did not receive sufficient information in advance of the arrival of a livestock vessel, thus they had to assess everything (e.g. stocking density plan and feed plan for the sea journey) once the vessel was in the port.

The official controls at the port are insufficient to minimise the risk of welfare problems for the animals involved in the journey. These are the result of under resourcing, insufficient planning (e.g. no sufficient time for vessel inspection), absence of detailed instructions and verification to trigger improvement.

The authorities have procedures for approval of the livestock vessels. Although these procedures include the network document translated to Croatian language, this has not been adapted to create suitable procedures and instructions to officials at the port. The instructions for staff to perform the vessel approval are not sufficient, which is not in line with Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The audit team noted that on 31 July 2018 the port veterinarians completed in one hour the preloading inspection of a large vessel used to carry over 3000 bovine animals (see also paragraph 23). For that vessel, it was unrealistic to complete a preloading inspection in just one hour.

The port veterinarians checked 78 loadings in 2017 and 40 loadings in the first semester of 2018. The reports of inspections did not indicate any deficiencies for vessels in the port in the last three years.

The veterinary inspector did not check the water production records or the working order of the drainage pump, alarms of the ventilation, fresh water and lighting systems5. This is not in line with Article 20(1)(c) of the Regulation. The procedures indicated the legal requirements for ventilation and alarms but did not indicate how to check these. The inspectors admitted that they were not competent to assess some of the "non-veterinary" requirements of the Regulation, such as the number of air exchanges required to provide sufficient ventilation.

The procedure indicates also the need for assessing the amount of feed, but not how to do it, conclude, record and report. The veterinarians generally relied on the agent's statement 5 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that " Inspection of the ventilation, alarm system, fresh water system and lighting system is carried out by the engineer of Ministry of Transport and infrastructure, Port authority-Pula at least 2 times a year, and when approving the ship jointly in cooperation with veterinary inspectors. After these checks, the veterinary inspector checks the functionality of all systems before loading, but does not perform detailed technical checks" 8 for this check. During the audit, the port veterinarian did some calculations on the spot during the loading. The audit team noted that procedures such as feeding plan could have been verified by the authorities in advance of the arrival of the vessel.

The inspectors confirmed to the audit team that they assess ventilation subjectively, based on their experience, and did not verify the air changes per hour required by Annex I Chapter IV, Section 1 point 2(a) of the Regulation.

The port veterinarians do not have the sufficient technical knowledge to perform a proper inspection of the livestock vessel and thus they do not assess effectively all the necessary elements. This, together with the short time allocated for the inspections, the absence of an approved classification society to verify the strength calculations of pen rails and decks indicates that the Croatian system to approve livestock vessels for transport in the EU and for inspecting them subsequently before each loading is insufficient to guarantee that animal welfare requirements are respected.

citations.text: The competent authority did not provide evidence that it has a procedure to verify the effectiveness and appropriateness of the official controls at the exit point, which is not in line with Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The majority of shortcomings detected during this audit were unknown to the authorities, e.g. that port veterinarians did not detect systematic deficiencies in journey logs (see paragraph 18) and procedures with insufficient detail for carrying out a practical assessment of requirements (see paragraph 34).

There were no reports on checks performed before November 2017. From November 2017 to May 2018 10 consignments were the subject of reports to the Member States of origin: one without one hour rest in the journey log, four that did not provide temperature records, three animals unfit for transport (two mastitis and one sick animal euthanised), one dead animal with no water in the vehicle and one with unsuitable dividers in the vehicle.

The audit team reviewed documentation of consignments arriving from five other Member States. None of them indicated who the sea transporter was. The audit team noted that: 5 In all journey logs seen, only organisers from one Member State had indicated the transfer of animals to a livestock vessel in box 6.1 of section 1. The logs from all other countries indicated the journeys ended at the port. However, in some journey logs the organisers indicated the name of the livestock vessel ­ so they had considered the journey out of the EU. But they failed to indicate the name and number of the authorised transporter responsible for this stage of the journey in box 6.4 of section 1 of the journey log. Only one Member State included the length of the sea journey in the total expected duration of the journey.

During four days, 101 trucks from five Member States arrived at the port during a heatwave to load cattle in a vessel that departed in August 2018. For those 101 trucks, veterinary inspectors detected that: in 26% of the trucks, animals had been exposed during the journeys to temperatures above 35oC; 6 16% of the truck drivers did not provided temperature records of the vehicles and 7% did not provided the journey logs; the journey planning, which is responsibility of the organisers, did not avoid the arrival of vehicles at the same time; daytime temperatures were well over 30oC, and thus the loading of vehicles at departure should not have been carried out if authorities there had checked the weather forecast for the port.

In that incident, the port veterinarians and representatives from the central authority did not have a clear course of action to follow to deal with the animals already in the port and those on their way4. After this incident the Croatian authorities notified three Member States by e-mail and for the other two Member States issued section V of the journey logs. Only one Member State replied to the Croatian contact point.

After this incident the Croatian authorities requested better coordination, scheduling and communication to all interested parties (shipping agent, port operator and main road transporter). During the closing meeting of this audit, the central authority stated that they will improve the related procedures.

The central authority indicated that they did not impose sanctions in relation to this incident. In their opinion, the detected infringements were caused by the lack of proper planning in the countries of departure of the consignments. They indicated they have a procedure that allows any vehicle to be detained until the fine is paid.

The authorities provided a document with the financial penalties for infringements to the Regulation. These range from HRK 10,000 (EUR 1,347) to HRK 100,000 (EUR 13,476). The average daily rental of a livestock vessel is EUR 25,000. The central authority indicated during the closing meeting that they plan to have new rules for sanctions next year. Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port

The official controls at the port are insufficient to minimise the risk of welfare problems for the animals involved in the journey. These are the result of under resourcing, insufficient planning (e.g. no sufficient time for vessel inspection), absence of detailed instructions and verification to trigger improvement.

As the authorities have not established a verification procedure over the official controls at the port, they are unable to detect and correct the existing weaknesses in their checks; 4 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that "During the incident a decision was made to load the animals on the ship, as the competent authority considered that returning the animals by road transport to the place of origin would cause additional animal suffering due to the weather conditions". 7 non-conformities persist undetected and thus are not communicated to the authorities of the Member States of departure. All this hinders continuous improvement to ensure the welfare of animals during transport.

recommendations.text: The competent authority should ensure that, for each sea consignment planned, there are arrangements to care for the animals and protect their welfare when the loading or sailing of a livestock vessel cannot take place, as required by Articles 22(2) and 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005.

citations.text: At the port, there was a single veterinary official in charge of many tasks, some of which occurred simultaneously, e.g inspection of the ship, control of documents from arriving trucks, assessment of fitness of animals. As result, not all tasks were completed properly and with the necessary attention.

The capacity of the assembly centre is not sufficient to accommodate all the animals loaded onto certain livestock vessels. In most cases, this is not a problem as the authorities co-ordinate the arrival of the trucks to the port and there are no major delays in transferring animals from road vehicles to the vessels. However, this can constitute a major problem in a case where the authorities refuse the loading of a big vessel. The authorities did not have arrangements to unload, accommodate, feed and water the animals in such cases and safeguard their welfare. This is not in line with Article 22(2) and Article 23 of the Regulation.

Procedures do not indicate that it is responsibility of the organisers to ensure that the time of arrival at the port should not coincide with the arrival of other vehicles in order to minimise the waiting time inside the port. This issue had to be raised with the organisers concerned, as required by Article 5(3)(a) of the Regulation, are legally responsible for coordinating the different parts of the journey.

citations.text: The veterinary inspector did not check the water production records or the working order of the drainage pump, alarms of the ventilation, fresh water and lighting systems5. This is not in line with Article 20(1)(c) of the Regulation. The procedures indicated the legal requirements for ventilation and alarms but did not indicate how to check these. The inspectors admitted that they were not competent to assess some of the "non-veterinary" requirements of the Regulation, such as the number of air exchanges required to provide sufficient ventilation.

The procedure indicates also the need for assessing the amount of feed, but not how to do it, conclude, record and report. The veterinarians generally relied on the agent's statement 5 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that " Inspection of the ventilation, alarm system, fresh water system and lighting system is carried out by the engineer of Ministry of Transport and infrastructure, Port authority-Pula at least 2 times a year, and when approving the ship jointly in cooperation with veterinary inspectors. After these checks, the veterinary inspector checks the functionality of all systems before loading, but does not perform detailed technical checks" 8 for this check. During the audit, the port veterinarian did some calculations on the spot during the loading. The audit team noted that procedures such as feeding plan could have been verified by the authorities in advance of the arrival of the vessel.
The competent authorities indicated they only get information on completion of sea journeys if vessels return to the port and if they request information on incidences in the last five journeys.

The inspectors confirmed to the audit team that they assess ventilation subjectively, based on their experience, and did not verify the air changes per hour required by Annex I Chapter IV, Section 1 point 2(a) of the Regulation.

The port veterinarians do not have the sufficient technical knowledge to perform a proper inspection of the livestock vessel and thus they do not assess effectively all the necessary elements. recommendations.text: The competent authority should identify, for any sailings from Rasa port, any natural or legal person as the authorised transporter for the journey by sea, as required by Article 6(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005.

citations.text: The procedures did not indicate that there needs to be a transporter for the sea journey who is established, or in the case that the applicant is established in a non-EU country, represented in the Member State (Article 10(1) of the Regulation). As a result port inspectors did not detect the absence of an authorised transporter responsible for the journey by sea (which should be in box 6.4 of section 1 of the journey logs). In practice, the port veterinarians make all requests regarding fulfilling the legal requirements for the export of animals to a forwarding agent, or the captain of the livestock vessel, although the competent authority has not defined if either of these actors have any legal responsibilities in relation to the welfare of animals during transport.

The failure to identify any natural or legal person as the authorised transporter for the journey by sea is further risk for animal welfare. However, this is also the failure of the authorities of the other Member States who approved journey logs which did not indicate an authorised transporter for the sea journey.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls by the State Inspectorate consistently verify that feed business operators meet the requirements for hazard identification in their respective hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) plans, as regards feed materials and other ingredients.

citations.text: For the establishments listed in section 2 of this report, the auditor analysed the most recent inspection reports and interviewed the inspectors on the assessment of operators' HACCP plans. The auditor noted that the assessment of the hazard identification part of the HACCP-plan by the inspectors was not always comprehensive: 1) For feed additives in general, it was not always verified that only authorised substances are used in the manufacture of feed. 2) For feed additives produced by fermentation, the necessity to verify that only authorised strains of the microorganisms were used, was missed by all of the inspectors interviewed. 3) For feed additives of mineral origin and produced by chemical synthesis, the occurrence of certain chemical hazards (e.g. dioxins/polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), heavy metals) was omitted in some cases. 4) The carrier of vegetable origin in a premixture was not a subject to hazard identification and this was not spotted by the inspectors. 5) In some cases, hazards which were not justified were included in the HACCP-plan (e.g. melamine in domestically produced cereals). 6) In one case, the auditor noted that the operator's hazard identification was generic without the level of detail necessary for a proper hazard identification, while the inspector made a largely comprehensive assessment of the hazard identification. However, the failure of the operator to identify relevant hazards, as required by Article 6(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, was not reflected in the most recent inspection report seen. Consequently, the operator was not notified about those deficiencies and was thus not incentivised to rectify them.

The inspection planning system is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out on all operators regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency. However, the effectiveness of the official controls system is weakened by shortcomings in the competent authority's (a) assessment of operators' HACCP plans, (b) assessment of the adequacy of operators' tests on homogeneity of mixing and cross-contamination, and (c) verification of operators' compliance with labelling requirements. 6 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

citations.text: The official check of whether operators meet the legislative labelling requirements always forms part of the inspections. However, none of the inspectors mentioned legal acts authorising individual feed additives, which often contain additional labelling requirements. This led to several cases where some specific labelling information was missing on the labels seen and this was not spotted by the inspectors. 2) In two labels of premixtures, the stability conditions should have been mentioned in the directions for use for certain feed additives, as required by the respective authorisation acts. recommendations.text: To ensure that the classification of production areas, the monitoring of production areas for microbiological quality and the decisions taken following the microbiological monitoring are carried out in line with Articles 52(2) and (3), 56- 58, 61(2) and 62 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

citations.text: The audit team noted that some of the production areas contained several "production zones", which may have different classifications; other production areas did not have this division. The audit team noted that this could be a wrong use of terminology as all "production zones" had fixed location and boundaries, had at least one sampling point for microbiological quality monitoring and were individually monitored for E. coli. and therefore individually classified, which are requirements of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 for production areas. 10 In their response to the draft report, it was confirmed that the CVI cannot carry out checks on phytoplankton, and a certain number of samples are processed for biotoxins by the NRL. 11 In their response to the draft report, it was clarified that there is no need to include the requirement for official controls by the competent authority on the operation of official and reference laboratories in the contract signed between the CVI and the IOF, because it is already prescribed by other MoA regulations. 5

In order to classify production areas (or "production zones" in those production areas that are further divided), the competent authorities did not fix a review period for sampling data in order to determine compliance with the requirements for class A, B and C areas, contrary to Article 52(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. National legislation established the conditions for reviewing the classification of the areas: in general, a result over the expected limits for a given class triggered a new sampling on the seventh and tenth day. The downgrade of classification only took place if one of these results, or if one result of the following months' regular monitoring samples, resulted over the expected limits. The downgrade was reverted if results were within the expected limit during three consecutive months. These conditions of Croatian national legislation do not allow an adequate classification of production areas, therefore production areas may be classified as A, B and C without meeting the corresponding standards of Articles 53- 55 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

The MoA has not started carrying out sanitary surveys in production areas (or "production zones" in those production areas that are further divided), contrary to Article 56(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

The monitoring plan established the requirements for the sampling to check the microbiological quality of live bivalve molluscs, as required in Article 59(b) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. In particular, the monitoring plan established: The sampling frequency, which was monthly in all production areas (or "production zones" in those production areas that are further divided). The periodicity is in line with the above-mentioned EURL guidance document. 12 The guidance document of the EU Reference Laboratory for monitoring bacteriological and viral contamination of bivalve molluscs ("Good Practice Guide; issue 7", December 2018). 6 The location of the sampling points. The competent authority designated these points years ago but there was no robust basis to support their locations. It could not be ensured that they were representative of the production areas, contrary to Article 61(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 and, therefore, they were of limited value. In addition, until sanitary surveys are completed, the monitoring plan is not in line with Articles 57 and 58 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The sampling method, including sampling at different depths when molluscs are farmed in ropes. The audit team found the method adequate for samples intended for microbiological analysis. The bivalve mollusc species, which was aquaculture mussel when this species was available. The plan did not consider sampling other mollusc species available in the same geographical location, either aquaculture oysters in the same area or natural beds in overlapping production areas. Therefore, and partly due to the lack of sanitary surveys, the competent authority did not take into account the likely variation in faecal contamination between different molluscs species, contrary to Article 61(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. b) For the presence of toxin-producing plankton in water

As explained in point 10 of this report, in general, a result over the expected limits for a given class triggered a new sampling on the seventh and tenth day. The downgrade of classification only took place if one of these results or if one result of the following months' regular monitoring samples, had a result over the expected limits. The downgrade was reverted if results were within the expected limit during three consecutive months. This is contrary to Article 52(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, based on which this reversion should only take place if the evaluation of the results available for the review period determine compliance with the corresponding standards. b) For the presence of toxin-producing plankton in water

The competent authority has established the location and boundaries of "production zones", monitors them individually for microbiological quality and classifies them. They conform to the EU concept of production areas, but the use of the term "production zones" is misleading.

The current classification of production areas (or "production zones" in those production areas that are further divided) is not in line with the EU requirements. This poses certain doubts that the level of contamination of molluscs harvested corresponds to the value expected according to their classification. In addition, as the plan does not consider sampling other mollusc species available in the same geographical location, this generates a risk of misclassification of the corresponding areas.

The lack of sanitary surveys questions the validity of the designated sampling points for microbiological monitoring and their representativeness for production areas, which has direct implications in the adequate classification of production areas.

The fact that the competent authority: does not close or reclassify the production area when certain regulatory limits for microbiological quality are exceeded for the first time, has not established review periods, and reverts the downgrade of classification with a few good results, may result in the placing on the market of bivalve molluscs with amounts of E. coli higher than the permitted ones, therefore being a potential risk for consumers.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the monitoring of production areas for presence of toxin-producing plankton is carried out in line with Articles 61(1), (3) and (7) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

citations.text: The monitoring plan established the requirements for the sampling of water to check for the presence of toxin-producing plankton in production areas, as required in Article 59(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. In particular, the monitoring plan established: The sampling frequency for water, which was weekly except from December to March, when it was fortnightly (due to the absence of biotoxins episodes, according to the explanation provided). The weekly periodicity was adequate but the evidence presented to support fortnightly sampling did not provide a robust basis for this decision: the audit team noted at least two results over the limit for biotoxins (one of PSP and one of lipophilic toxin) during these winter months. Peaks of plankton preceding biotoxin episodes can go unnoticed in between two samplings. The location of the sampling points. These points were located inside production areas, coinciding with sampling points for biotoxins. Therefore, they were of limited value as early warnings suggesting an accumulation of biotoxins, and are not representative, contrary to Article 61(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. The sampling method, which consisted of a 20 microns mesh diameter net, pulled vertically from the bottom to the surface. This method was adequate for qualitative purposes as it filtered larger amounts of water and, therefore, concentrated the number of phytoplankton cells (the IOF provided data collected in 2007 that show higher accumulation of cells using this net) and it could complement a quantitative method. However, the vertical pulling of the net does not allow the collection of a representative sample of the water column, contrary to Article 61(7) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627. 7 The persons that could collect samples. According to the information provided, in general, staff from the IOF took water samples, using the method described in the previous point (i.e. net). In remoter areas, authorized veterinarians took water samples. The audit team assessed a PSP episode that occurred in one of these remoter areas, and noted a very low number of the corresponding plankton species. Following the request of the audit team for an explanation on that, the IOF found that authorized veterinarians did not use the prescribed sampling method and they collected only surface water.

The IOF established the list of toxin-producing plankton species that had to be monitored, but did not determine thresholds for some of them. According to the information provided, these species were rare in the Croatian waters, but the audit team noted that laboratory results regularly reported a few of them (e.g. Alexandrium spp.). In addition, the laboratory did not consider the different toxicity of different species within the same genus (e.g. Dinophysis spp). c) For the presence of biotoxins in live bivalve molluscs

The official control system did not foresee any decisions following monitoring for the presence of toxin-producing plankton in water. In particular, it did not foresee an intensive sampling following results suggesting an accumulation of toxins in live bivalve mollusc flesh, contrary to Article 61(3)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

According to the information provided, the laboratory did not have to highlight results exceeding the limits when transmitting the test results to competent authorities. The laboratory did not have to transmit the results to other laboratories in charge of analyses for biotoxins either, although this could help the analyst to focus on potentially positive samples. c) For the presence of biotoxins in live bivalve molluscs

citations.text: Regarding the ASP laboratory reviewed: The laboratory validated and accredited this method in 2009 and it has not renewed the validation since then (according to the information provided, it was due to the considerable amount of certified reference material that it implied and the corresponding costs, and because there was no ASP in Croatian waters). The laboratory carried out the validation in mussels, although some of the samples tested in this laboratory were from other molluscs' species. This may have an impact on the testing results due to the potential matrix effect. The laboratory carried out the testing according to a SOP, using reference material tissue as internal quality control. However, the SOP did not reflect the actual identification and performance criteria used during the analysis. The participation in the last inter-comparison tests showed satisfactory results.

Regarding the PSP laboratory visited: The laboratory recently revalidated this method in December 2020. The accreditation of this method did not have within its scope all the compounds that this laboratory tested. The laboratory carried out the testing according to a SOP, and used only certified reference material. There were internal quality controls established for the method, tested in each sequence of analysis. The laboratory tested all the relevant PSP compounds, however the SOP did not reflect it (i.e. GTX 6 and C3, 4). The participation results of the last inter-comparison tests showed good results for total toxicity, but unsatisfactory results for STX in one of the three samples. The laboratory suspected a problem with the equipment but did not find a conclusive explanation for the result; therefore, it did not implement any corrective action. As the STX is the most toxic compound of this group, this could pose a risk of underestimation of PSP if an episode would occur.

Regarding the two lipophilic toxin laboratories reviewed: The laboratories validated and accredited this method in 2014 for all the compounds of the lipophilic toxin group. 15 The laboratories carried out the validation in mussels, although some of the samples tested in this laboratory were from other mollusc species. One of the laboratories recently started the revalidation of the method and the other laboratory scheduled a revalidation in 2021. In both cases, the revalidation was going to include other mollusc species, which is imperative in order to take into account the potential matrix effect in the testing results. The laboratories carried out the testing according to the corresponding laboratory SOP, using in both cases the certified reference materials commercially available for this toxin group to prepare calibration standards and internal quality controls. However, the SOPs did not include the performance criteria for internal quality controls. In one of the laboratories, the SOP did not reflect the formula for calculation of individual toxin concentrations, and in the other, it did not include the identification criteria for certain compounds. The results of participation in the last inter-comparison tests showed unsatisfactory and questionable results for some of the compounds/individual toxins of this group. Both laboratories suspected a problem with the sample matrix but did not find a conclusive explanation for this result. This could pose a risk of underestimation of the lipophilic toxin group when an episode occurs (the lipophilic toxin group is the most common biotoxin in Croatian waters).

Although laboratories have validated the analytical methods, a validation carried out more than a decade ago or the use of a method validated for one species when analysing a different one may diminish its significance.
The fact that not all the PSP compounds that laboratories test are included in the scope of accreditation of the method diminishes the reliability of those tests results.

Laboratories provide, in principle, reliable results but there is certain risk of underestimation of biotoxins as laboratories did not find conclusive explanations for unsatisfactory and questionable results in proficiency tests.

recommendations.text: To ensure that National Reference Laboratories effectively comply with the tasks and responsibilities established in Article 101(1)(b), (c) and (e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and that the Ministry of Agriculture organises audits to official laboratories they have designated (including National Reference Laboratories), as required by Article 39(1) of the same Regulatio (second and third bullet points).

citations.text: According to national legislation, and in line to Article 101(1)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, National Reference Laboratories (NRLs) had to provide scientific and technical assistance to the competent authority. However, currently they provided scarce assistance to the MoA (e.g. regarding the designation of sampling points or the species to be sampled) and of limited value for developing the monitoring plan for the production areas. 8 Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 on the hygiene of foodstuffs. 9 Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 29 April 2004 laying down specific hygiene rules for food of animal origin. 4

Since 20019, the MoA has not carried out audits of official laboratories, contrary to the requirement of Article 39 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Every year, the MoA signs a contract with the CVI, which designates two of its laboratories as official controls laboratories for the implementation of the monitoring plan of production areas. Traditionally, the CVI subcontracts part of the biotoxin analyses to the IOF. Although the original contract foresees the possibility of subcontracting, this may only occur where the CVI itself is not able to ensure the implementation of the plan. The audit team had doubts about the need for subcontracting biotoxin analyses as the two CVIs designated are fully equipped and receive a limited number of samples per week (nine on average, see points 55-58), but the CVI explained that subcontracting to the IOF is in line with the internal organisation of the activities of the CVI and MoA10. The subcontracting contract does not contain certain legal requirements that are included in the original contract signed between MoA and CVI (e.g. the official controls by the competent authority on the operation of official and reference laboratories)11.

The national legislation that incorporates the EU requirements is obsolete and does not correctly interpret some of these requirements, which is of particular relevance in relation to the decisions that the competent authority takes subsequent to the monitoring of production areas for microbiological quality. The MoA, which designs the monitoring plan that is the basis for the official control of production areas, has a reduced oversight of the sector. This is partly due to the currently significant lack of input from NRLs into the monitoring plan. All this has a negative impact in the effectiveness of the control of production areas.

Regarding the NRL: This laboratory did not prepare inter-comparison tests but it requested to the EURL the participation of the two other official control laboratories in the EURL annual proficiency testing. There was no established frequency; their participation depended on the availability of samples at the EURL. According to the information provided for one of the biotoxins as an example, one of the laboratories participated every year since 2014. Due to the pandemic in 2020, the laboratories did not participate in a proficiency testing in 2020. The result of the 2019 proficiency testing indicated that the two official control laboratories could not always detect all the compounds of the PSP group. It also showed questionable or unsatisfactory results for a few of the PSP compounds and for some of the compounds of the lipophilic toxin group. This may lead to a potential underestimation of these toxins if an episode would occur. The NRL asked laboratories to carry out a follow-up of these results, but only closer support would ensure the appropriate follow-up that Article 101(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 requires. Apart from requesting follow-up of questionable or unsatisfactory proficiency testing results, the audit team did not find evidence of implementation of Article 101(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, regarding the responsibilities of NRLs to coordinate the activities of official laboratories with a view of improving the methods of laboratory analysis. 16 Conclusions on laboratories

The NRL for biotoxins is not entirely fulfilling all its responsibilities and tasks, which can affect negatively the harmonisation and improvement in the performance of testing methods by other official laboratories and the competence of staff when using these complex analytical methods.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the national legislation facilitates the immediate implementation of eradication measures, in line with the requirements of Article 17(1) and (4) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, and are implemented immediately, as well as the efficient and effective coordination between all CAs involved, as required under Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The following legislation and guidelines are relevant in the context of the audit: 4 · The Croatian Plant Health Act (Official Gazette of the Republic of Croatia (OG, No. 127/19) implements Regulation (EU) 2016/2031 and lays down the division of competences for the performance of official controls in the field of plant health, and the rights and powers of phytosanitary and forestry inspectors responsible for official controls in this area. According to Article 5 of this act, the MA is responsible for the coordination of these matters, and under its Article 7 the MA is responsible for establishing a DA when a positive finding of the pest is confirmed. The MA and the SI explained to the audit team that they disagree on whether or not this act provides the necessary legal basis for the SI to take immediate actions when a positive finding of the pest is confirmed. In the view of the SI, they do not have the legal basis to implement eradication measures until the MA has established a DA, while the MA considers that the SI can take measures when a priority pest is confirmed, even before a DA has been established. This disagreement contributed to the delay in implementing eradication measures in 2019, further described under section 5.4. The inability to find a solution to a fundamental issue indicates a lack of coordination between the CAs involved, contrary to Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, according to which Member States shall ensure the efficient and effective coordination between all CAs involved and the consistency of the official activities. · Decision on the designation of demarcated areas where measures are implemented to prevent the spread of A. chinensis (OG, No. 13/20). The decision is adopted by the MA and is updated when necessary. · The National plan for the annual surveys for A. chinensis and eight other pests, drawn up by the MA, forms the basis for surveys carried out in pest-free areas and in DAs. · The Action Plan to control and prevent the spread of A. chinensis for the period 2022-2025, adopted in 2022. The Action Plan describes the measures to be taken in DAs to eradicate the pest, the division of competencies between the CAs, the training of operators and information to the public. It does however not include a time schedule for the application of the eradication measures, contrary to the requirements of Article 27(1) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. The plan further lays down that the felling of specified plants in the infested zone (IZ) may be exempted if it is possible to carry out individual recording and mapping of these plants every month from May to September. While this is in line with the applicable EU legislation, EU law also requires that the exemption is for exceptional cases where a responsible official body concludes that such felling is inappropriate, and that measures to prevent any possible spread of the pest from those plants must be applied. These elements are not included in the Action Plan, hence it does not correspond to the requirements as laid down in Annex II, section 3(1)(b) of Decision (EU) 2012/138. 5 5.1.3 Documented control procedures and audits

The plant health controls are carried out by designated authorities, mainly in line with EU and national legislation, but the disagreement concerning the interpretation of the legislation indicates poor coordination between the MA and the SI and has contributed to delays in the implementation of the applicable EU legislation.

During the on-site visit in the DA of Jankolovica, the audit team noted that specified plants remained also in this IZ. The SI explained to the audit team that in this case the reason was the Croatian legislation concerning felling of trees, according to which the owner is responsible for the felling and must at least be informed before any tree is felled. According to the SI, the task of identifying and getting in contact with the owner was time consuming and not possible in some cases. To leave specified trees in the IZ for an undefined time is not in accordance with Annex II, section 3(1)(b) of Decision (EU) 2012/138, and the inability to take immediate eradication measures when the pest is present on private premises is contrary to the requirements of Article 17(4) of Regulation (EC) 2016/2031. 5.5.3 Destruction of plants

The requirement to contact owners before felling trees in combination with the inability of the CA to swiftly identify these owners, leads to delays in the felling of specified plants in the IZs increasing the risks for the continued spread of the pest.

recommendations.text: To ensure that specially registered FBOs comply with the requirements of Article 1.5.(b).(ii) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004 in relation to the obligation to have a "localised" activity.

citations.text: However, registered businesses are allowed to trade their products in the whole territory of Croatia, which is not in line with the requirements of Article 1.5.(b).(ii) of Regulation (EC) No 853/2004.

recommendations.text: To urgently address the lack of specific training provided to control staff, of adequate supervision (internal audit) and the limited coordination between the CAs in order to provide sufficient guarantees that consistent enforcement and action following official controls are always carried out.

citations.text: The central office of SI ­ Independent Internal Audit Service (staffed with 3 auditors) also carries out the supervision of the work of the DBs entrusted with official controls: supervision is carried out by documentary checks at the DB headquarters, with a limited component performed by witness audit in the field. No internal audit in the dairy sector had been performed in the recent years (the last audit in the veterinary field was carried out in 2024 on official sampling of poultry caecum, involving 10 DBs and 1 witness au- dit in the field).

Staff of DBs had not been provided with specific training since a long time: some years ago an online training on HACCP in dairy had been provided but not sufficiently de- tailed on the verification/validation of the milk heat-treatment process. Moreover, AVs of DBs have to deal with a large number of FBOs involved in the processing of different commodities (meat, milk, fish, retail, etc.), making it hard to be specialised in any of them. Due to this lack of training and of some specific knowledge required in the dairy processing sector, the effectiveness of the official controls carried out by DBs is also sometimes questionable.
The SI organises at least twice a year a co-ordination meeting between Veterinary and Sanitary Inspection. Coordination activities between VFSI and VFSD had not been doc- umented.

The VFSD have a formal computerised reporting system in place for the outcome of official controls (approval/registration processes, animal health controls) called VetIs, to which also the VFSI has access. This latter uses its own database e-Inspector for reporting of official controls, for its exclusive use (the VFSD has no access to this database). Conclusions on competent authorities
Limited and insufficient training impact the technical knowledge of the control staff and, ultimately, on the effectiveness of official controls.
The lack of adequate supervision (internal audit) and the limited coordination between CAs do not provide sufficient guarantees that consistent enforcement and actions are always carried out.

citations.text: All visited establishments had a valid approval at the time of the audit team visit. How- ever, also discrepancies were noted: a. some FBOs had not informed the CAs about relevant changes that had occurred in the structure/equipment/activities, as required by Article 6.2 of Reg. 852/2004, and by Article 9 of Rules on the registration and approval of establishments and registration of operators in food businesses (OG 123/19). No specific sanctions had been applied by the VFSI staff in such cases; b. in one of the holdings visited, the operator had not informed the CA on the ceased operation of sale of raw milk through 3 vending machines: the operator has been sanctioned by VFSI Decision on 18 March 2025; c. in one establishment one storage building and two new reception silos for raw milk had been added later (in 2024) to the original layout; however, the approval was not amended because the new premises lacked the approval/license of the SI ­ Sector of Building Inspection (to note that the entire site was not fenced). The VFSD requested in writing specific information on the case to the SI­ Sector of Building Inspection, but no response was received. As a results, the VFSI inspec- tor requested the unapproved parts not to be used until their full approval: howev- er, both the storage building (with packaging material for the use by the sister company stored inside) and the two silos for the raw milk (clean, but with smell of fresh milk) were already occasionally used by the FBO without the inspector be- ing aware of this; d. some activities performed in another establishment visited (butter, fresh cheese, cottage cheese) were not included in the approval; 8 e. approval of establishments, to which flexibility options had been granted, had been done without adequate verification of the actual conditions (including sepa- ration in time of specific operations) and FBO's self-control system (simplified HACCP/GHP). No specific prescriptions concerning separation in time/in space had been included in the approval conditions, in order to ensure hygienic pro- cessing conditions.

The provisions and procedures in place for the registration and/or approval of dairy businesses are adequate to maintain oversight over the approval conditions. However, the current approvals granted to FBOs do not always ensure that all activities and struc- tures are covered by a valid approval.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the scope of the accreditation of the official laboratories include those methods of laboratory analysis, test or diagnosis required to be used by the laboratory for analyses, tests or diagnoses of those pests included in the multi-annual survey programme, in line with Article 37(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The NRL is EN ISO/IEC 17025 accredited for the determination of the following organisms; A. chinensis, Citrus tristeza virus, Clavibacter sepedonicus, Globodera rostochiensis and G. pallida, Phyllosticta citricarpa, Phytophthora ramorum, Plum pox virus, Ralstonia solanacearum and Thrips palmi. It has participated in interlaboratory testing for PWN in 2020 and 2023, P. japonica in 2023, and for Spodoptera frugiperda, T. palmi and Agrilus planipennis in 2024. For the multi-annual survey programme which includes more than 400 species (see Chapter 5.2), the limited number of pests included in the accreditation is not fully in line with the requirements of Article 37(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. This Article requires that the scope of the accreditation of an official laboratory, shall include those methods of laboratory analysis, test or diagnosis required to be used by the laboratory for analyses, tests or diagnoses, when it operates as an official laboratory.

The NRL has a quality assurance system in place. This laboratory is accredited and has participated in interlaboratory testing for the determination of some priority and EU quarantine pests. Nevertheless, the incomplete accreditation for the remaining methods required for the multi-annual survey programme, reduces the level of assurance in their respective survey results.

recommendations.text: Ensure that a statistically based annual survey programme based on the level of risk is established and implemented for Xylella fastidiosa, as required by Article 2(3) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. Ensure that this annual survey takes into account the European Food Safety Authority Guidelines for statistically sound and risk-based surveys of this pest in the survey design and the sampling scheme for all parts of Croatia, in line with Article 2(4) of the above EU Regulation.

citations.text: The CAAF informed the audit team that several counties of Croatia which have X. fastidiosa host plants, but environmental conditions with a low risk, are not taken into account in the survey for this pest. The design of the survey system practically assigns a zero risk to these areas, rather than a low risk. This is not in line with the environmental suitability factors, as described in the EFSA Guidelines and therefore, not fully in line with Article 2(3) and (4) of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 which, requires that surveys shall be performed on the basis of the level of risk. Additionally, islands which have difficult access are not part of the survey programme for the presence of X. fastidiosa. This is not in line with Article 2(3) of the same Regulation.

The SI also surveys in Croatia for the presence of X. fastidiosa. Planning of these surveys is done by assigning the staff available to maximise the number of inspections. The responsible staff from the SI informed the audit team that these surveys are not statistically based, contrary to the requirements of Article 2(4) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. The SI surveys garden centres and nurseries in four inland counties. Urban areas and crops are surveyed in another five counties. For the 2024 survey season, the SI planned to survey 36 nurseries and garden centres, 28 urban areas and 17 fields, taking a total of 105 samples. For the current 2025 season, the SI is planning to survey a total of 90 sites and take 115 samples.

For the implementation of the 2024 annual survey plan for X. fastidiosa, the PHD reported that CAAF and SI have implemented 408 visual inspections, 35 of which were implemented in nurseries. The same CAs took 297 samples during the 2024 season, of these 115 were taken in garden centres. Although the sampling target was fully achieved, concerning the number of sites visited and samples taken (see paragraph 22 and 23), it is not possible to determine the confidence level achieved by this survey at national level (see paragraph 21 and 23).

The multi-annual survey programme for the relevant Union quarantine pests (including relevant priority pests) provides a basis for the early detection of any outbreaks of these pests. The small number of shortcomings identified do not have a critical impact on the outcome of the survey programmes.

recommendations.text: Ensure that surveys for the presence of Bursaphelenchus xylophilus are annually carried out on vectors in line Article 2(1) of Implementing Decision 2012/535/EU.

citations.text: The CAAF has 20 pheromone traps to capture beetles of the genus Monochamus sp. while the CFRI has 28. The beetles captured are tested at the CFRI (see paragraph 3) to determine whether they belong to any non-European species, which are EU quarantine pests. However, they are not examined for the presence of PWN, contrary to the requirements of Article 2(1) of Implementing Decision 2012/535/EU which requires that, MS shall annually conduct surveys for Bursaphelenchus xylophilus on the vector.

For the 2024 annual survey for PWN, the CFRI visited seven counties, and performed 2 610 visual examinations of individual trees. Field inspectors visited 32 forest units and took 28 samples of wood, exceeding the annual plan. The CFRI reported that surveys focussed on symptomatic trees of Pinus halepensis by the coastal counties and Pinus sylvestris in the non-coastal ones. CFRI captured 130 Monochamus sp. beetles in the 29 pheromone traps placed. These beetles were analysed at the CFRI laboratory to determine whether they belonged to non-European species. However, they were not tested for the presence of PWN (see paragraph 30).

In 2024, the CAAF visited 5 counties and took 25 samples of wood from forest stands and public areas near ports. This CA reported captured 10 Monochamus sp. beetles which were examined with the same objective as the beetles captured by the CFRI.

The multi-annual survey programme for the relevant Union quarantine pests (including relevant priority pests) provides a basis for the early detection of any outbreaks of these pests. The small number of shortcomings identified do not have a critical impact on the outcome of the survey programmes.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the CAs regularly review and, where appropriate, update their contingency plans in line with Article 25(4) of Regulations (EU) 2016/2031, and consult all relevant stakeholders in the process of keeping up to date the contingency plans in line with Article 25(1) of the same EU Regulation.

citations.text: The contingency plans are overall in line with the requirements of Article 25(2) of Regulations (EU) 2016/2031. All CAs participated in the drafting of the plans (see paragraph 2 and 3) however, they have not consulted the relevant stakeholders in the process of drawing up and keeping up to date the contingency plans. This is contrary to the requirements of Article 25(1) of Regulations (EU) 2016/2031.

The CAs informed the audit team that they are considering how to amend the national legislation to address these issues. Once they are addressed, the CAs can review these plans, which is a requirement under Article 25(4) of Regulation (EU) 2016/2031. Conclusions on contingency plans

By developing all required contingency plans, Croatia has laid down a solid basis to eradicate any outbreak of relevant EU priority pests. Once the shortcomings identified in the simulation exercises are addressed, the CAs will be able to rapidly implement eradication measures in the case of an outbreak of a priority pest.

audits.title: evaluate the implementation of official controls on feed hygiene

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls by the State Inspectorate are capable of verifying that feed business operators meet the requirements for appropriate and regular checks of the effectiveness of mixing (homogeneity).
recommendations.legal_basis: part 3(b) of section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

citations.text: In four establishments visited, tests to assess the homogeneity of mixing were carried out at least every five years. The contracted laboratory used the statistical program provided by the manufacturer of the tracer particles, however, wrongly performed the statistical analysis - a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test for homogeneity - based on the raw values of the optical density measurements (in general < 5) and not as required by the software by analysing the calculated amount of tracer particles per sample (in general > 200). When conducting a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test, low expected counts (e.g. <5) not only violate the chi-squared approximation assumptions but also directly reduce the test's power to detect inhomogeneous mixing. In one example the auditors noted that a coefficient of variation of 58.6% resulted wrongly in the conclusion that the mixing was effective regarding the homogeneity. Accordingly, the scrutinised tests for homogeneity of mixing were not in line with the requirements laid down by part 3(b) of section "Facilities and equipment" of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 and this was overlooked during previous official inspections.

The inspection planning system is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out on all operators regularly, on a risk basis and with appropriate frequency. While feed inspectors regularly use checklists and guidance documents and official inspections are documented, the effectiveness of the official controls system is weakened by shortcomings in the competent authority's assessment of the adequacy of operators' tests on homogeneity of mixing. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 Planning of official sampling

recommendations.text: To ensure that the test results interpretation approach for determining sampling- related non-compliances does take into account all of the relevant factors set out in the legislation.

citations.text: The auditor team noted in several sampling-related non-compliances in compound feed for broiler chicken identified between 2022 and 2024 that the non-compliance decisions were wrongly based on unavoidable carry-over of coccidiostats in non-target feed exceeding maximum allowed levels (Section VII of Directive 2022/32/EC). However, the respective coccidiostats were listed on the product labels of the compound feeds as authorised feed additives. The audit team established as well that in these sampling-related non-compliances the measured concentration of coccidiostats was significantly smaller than (i) declared on the label, and (ii) the respective allowed concentration range as defined in the authorisation. However, these non-compliances were overlooked by the SI's inspectors and the Croatian Veterinary Institute's laboratory. These findings are not in line with the legal requirements of Article 15(e) and (f) of Regulation (EC) 767/2009. Conclusion on the planning and implementation of official sampling

Many aspects of the planning and implementation of sampling and testing of official feed samples are positive. The risk-based approach adopted for the planning of official sampling, its implementation, and availability of suitable sampling equipment ensure official samples' legal and technical validity. However, the test results interpretation approach for determining sampling-related non-compliances does not take into account all the relevant factors set out in the legislation affecting the legal validity of these decisions made on non-compliant samples, and thus weakens the overall effectiveness of the official controls. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances
